summary: New box Part. Pass.: example for sense 1 in Part. Pass. (MAC NE Samson the hero/22)

data.turoyo: Azzé mbele. Hooo, komqašməri aʕle, ʕayne kanné biṭe, iḏoṯe kanné mәṣre, ŭ zənǧər harke ŭ harke, ha hawxa kanné iḏe mәṣre bu+zənǧər.
data.translation: He went to take him. Oooh, they mock at him, his eyes, there they are, burst, his hands, there they are bound, and a chain, here and here, just like so, there are his hands, tied with the chain.

rationale: New Detransitive Part. Pass. box; plural state biṭe parallels bound hands.

data.translation: They went, they threw themselves into the pond. Some, their legs broke. Some, their arms broke. Some, their eyes burst. Some, became sick and diseased.

summary: All 24 records checked. Active l-agent forms denote causing rupture; Detransitive forms denote rupture without a syntactically expressed causer, even when poison, injury or an earlier attack motivates it.
mibəṭ at 91/14 is Infectum, despite inclusion in an example filed as Detransitive Preterit. The paired negative biṭ is Preterit; preserve the existing complex quotation.

biṭe at MAC Samson/22 supports a new Part. Pass. box through plural state morphology and parallel bound-hands predication. bәṭṭo at Lahdo snake/8 is uncertain and does not independently license a new box.
No distinct new numbered sense or new idiom is justified. The main revision clarifies transitive valency already present in the entry.
Legacy Prym–Socin citations are not changed merely because supplied text/verse references differ.
Confirm whether bәṭṭo at Lahdo snake/8 is a phonetic/transcription variant of biṭo or a separate adjective; the implicit affected subject may switch from nail to finger.
Confirm Part. Pass. plural biṭe versus finite plural -i in the Samson dialect.
Check agreement of biṭo with ʕaynayye and the referent of ṭḥolo at 113/99 against source or speaker; no new medical sense is inferred.
Map legacy PrS references to supplied text/verse citations before changing them.
Wrong case in German: ihm → ihn
rationale: The construction is jemanden zum Aufplatzen bringen; the foot is the accusative object. The supplied edition repeats ihm, but the German case error is independently clear.
